Origen of Alexandria
Greek Church Father; Alexandrian theologian

Origen was the most important early proponent of allegorical and spiritual interpretation. In On First Principles (II.11) he criticized those who expect a material kingdom of eating, drinking and rebuilt Jerusalem, arguing that the promises refer to spiritual realities. His approach strongly influenced the decline of chiliasm in the Greek East and anticipates the idealist approach to Revelation. Some of his speculative views (such as the restoration of all things) were later condemned.
Eusebius of Caesarea
Greek Church Father; bishop and church historian

Eusebius, the 'father of church history', preserves much of our knowledge of early eschatological debate. His Ecclesiastical History quotes Papias and reports the debate over Revelation's authorship, including Dionysius of Alexandria's doubts, and records Irenaeus's statement dating Revelation to Domitian's reign. He was hostile to chiliasm and saw Constantine's Christian empire as a fulfilment of God's purposes, an outlook sometimes called an early 'realized' or imperial eschatology.
Tertullian
Latin Church Father (Carthage); later associated with Montanism

Tertullian, the first major Latin theologian, affirmed in Against Marcion (III.24) a thousand-year kingdom on earth after the resurrection in a divinely built Jerusalem, distinct from the heavenly kingdom that follows. He also wrote on the resurrection of the flesh against those who spiritualized it. His later sympathy for the Montanist movement, with its intense expectation of the New Jerusalem, made chiliasm suspect for some later writers.
James M. Hamilton Jr.
Southern Baptist; Southern Baptist Theological Seminary biblical theologian

Hamilton is a biblical theologian whose work centres on God's glory in salvation through judgment. He defended historic premillennialism at the 2009 Desiring God panel and in his preaching commentary on Revelation. With Fred Zaspel he argued in Three Views on Israel and the Church for a future mass conversion of ethnic Israel without a separate role for Israel apart from the church.
Francisco Ribera
Spanish Jesuit

Ribera's commentary on Revelation (c. 1590) placed most of the book (after the opening chapters) in the future, immediately before Christ's return, with a personal Antichrist reigning three and a half years. Protestant historians often describe this as a Counter-Reformation reply to the Protestant identification of the papacy with Antichrist. Modern futurists generally acknowledge him as an early systematic futurist while noting that futurist elements go back to Irenaeus and Hippolytus.
Luis de Alcázar

Alcázar's Vestigatio Arcani Sensus in Apocalypsi (1614) is usually cited as the first systematic preterist commentary on Revelation. He read the early chapters as the church's victory over Judaism (the fall of Jerusalem) and the later chapters as its victory over pagan Rome. Protestant historians often describe his work, like Ribera's, as a Counter-Reformation alternative to the historicist papal-Antichrist reading; preterists note that preterist readings of individual texts are much older.
William Milligan
Church of Scotland; University of Aberdeen

Milligan was a Scottish Presbyterian scholar whose lectures and Expositor's Bible volume on Revelation are classic statements of the idealist (spiritual) approach. He argued that Revelation is not a calendar of events but a symbolic portrayal of principles governing the conflict between Christ and evil throughout the church age. His approach influenced later amillennial commentators.
Tyconius
North African Donatist lay theologian

Tyconius wrote the Book of Rules, the first Latin handbook of biblical interpretation, and a now-lost commentary on Revelation. He read the Apocalypse spiritually as a description of the church throughout the present age, including the present binding of Satan and the 'first resurrection' as spiritual renewal. Augustine adopted and transmitted many of his ideas, making Tyconius a key source for later amillennial and idealist interpretation.
Lactantius
Latin Christian apologist; tutor to Constantine's son

Lactantius's Divine Institutes, Book VII, contains one of the fullest early Christian accounts of the end: the world lasting six thousand years, a final tyrant, the return of Christ, and a seventh millennium of earthly peace and abundance before the final judgment. He represents the strong chiliastic tradition in the Latin West before Tyconius and Augustine reshaped it.
David Chilton
Reformed; Christian Reconstruction movement

Chilton was a Reconstructionist pastor whose Paradise Restored offered a popular biblical theology of dominion and The Days of Vengeance a full-length partial-preterist, postmillennial commentary on Revelation as a covenant lawsuit against apostate Jerusalem. Late in life he adopted full preterism, though he did not publish a full defense of it; his earlier works remain widely used by partial preterists.
J. Marcellus Kik
Presbyterian pastor and editor

Kik's An Eschatology of Victory (published posthumously in 1971) combined a preterist exposition of Matthew 24 with a postmillennial reading of Revelation 20. He argued that the dividing line in Matthew 24 falls at verse 35 (or 36), with everything before it fulfilled in AD 70. His work influenced later writers such as Gentry and DeMar.
John MacArthur
Non-denominational Reformed-leaning evangelical; Grace Community Church and The Master's Seminary

MacArthur pastored Grace Community Church in Sun Valley, California, for over five decades and led The Master's Seminary. His 2007 Shepherds' Conference address argued that consistent Calvinists should be premillennialists, since God's sovereign, unconditional election of Israel guarantees his promises to the nation. He held a pretribulational rapture and future millennium, while distancing himself from some traditional dispensational distinctives. Sam Waldron and others published replies.
Tim LaHaye
Baptist pastor; co-founder of the Pre-Trib Research Center

LaHaye was a pastor and author who, with Jerry B. Jenkins, wrote the Left Behind novels, which brought a pretribulational dispensational scenario to tens of millions of readers. He co-founded the Pre-Trib Research Center with Thomas Ice to defend futurism scholarly and co-edited The End Times Controversy against preterism. Critics such as Hank Hanegraaff targeted his approach as sensationalist; supporters credit him with renewing interest in prophecy and evangelism.
Mark Hitchcock
Dispensational Bible church pastor; Dallas Theological Seminary

Hitchcock is a pastor and popular dispensational writer on prophecy who wrote his doctoral dissertation defending the late (Domitianic) date of Revelation against preterist arguments. With Thomas Ice he wrote Breaking the Apocalypse Code in reply to Hank Hanegraaff. His many popular books argue for a pretribulational rapture and a future seven-year tribulation.
Hal Lindsey
Dispensational evangelical; Dallas Theological Seminary graduate

Lindsey's The Late Great Planet Earth (1970) became one of the best-selling non-fiction books of its decade by connecting dispensational prophecy to the Cold War, the 1948 founding of Israel and Middle East politics. It popularized the expectation that the generation that saw Israel's rebirth would see Christ's return. Scholarly dispensationalists have often distanced themselves from his date-oriented speculations; critics cite them as a cautionary example of 'newspaper exegesis'.
Hank Hanegraaff
Evangelical apologist ('Bible Answer Man'); Eastern Orthodox since 2017

Hanegraaff, longtime president of the Christian Research Institute, wrote The Apocalypse Code (2007), proposing an 'exegetical eschatology' that reads Revelation largely as fulfilled in the judgment on Jerusalem while affirming a future bodily return and resurrection. He sharply criticized the Left Behind scenario and Christian Zionism. Thomas Ice and Mark Hitchcock answered him in Breaking the Apocalypse Code. He joined the Eastern Orthodox Church in 2017.
Michael L. Brown
Messianic Jewish, charismatic evangelical; host of The Line of Fire

Brown is a Messianic Jewish scholar of Semitic languages and a radio host and debater. He holds a historic (non-dispensational) premillennial, posttribulational view, set out with Craig Keener in Not Afraid of the Antichrist. He strongly affirms a future for ethnic Israel and has debated Gary DeMar on 'replacement theology' and full preterists Don Preston and Michael Sullivan.
J. Stuart Russell
English Congregationalist minister

Russell's The Parousia (1878) is the classic Victorian argument that every New Testament prediction of Christ's coming was fulfilled within the generation ending in AD 70. He worked systematically through the time-statements of the Gospels, Epistles and Revelation. The book is foundational for modern full preterism and is also widely read by partial preterists, who accept its time-text arguments but reject its conclusions about the resurrection and final judgment.
The Meaning of the Millennium: Four Views

The classic evangelical multi-view volume on the millennium (InterVarsity Press). Each of four scholars sets out his position on Revelation 20 and the shape of the end, and the other three respond. It defined the four-way categories most later discussions use.
Ladd argues that Revelation 20 follows the Second Coming of Revelation 19 and that the two resurrections of Revelation 20:4-6 must both be bodily.
Hoyt defends dispensational premillennialism, stressing literal fulfilment of the covenants with national Israel.
Boettner argues that the gospel will Christianize the world through ordinary means before Christ returns.
Hoekema presents amillennialism as inaugurated eschatology: the millennium is the present reign of Christ and departed saints.
The responses show that hermeneutics (how literally to read prophecy and Revelation) drives most disagreements.
Three Views on the Millennium and Beyond

Zondervan Counterpoints volume in which a progressive dispensational premillennialist (Blaising), a postmillennialist (Gentry) and an amillennialist (Strimple) each present their case and respond to the others. It is often regarded as the most exegetically detailed of the millennial multi-view books.
Blaising frames premillennialism within a holistic 'new creation' eschatology that includes nations and Israel.
Gentry grounds postmillennialism in the Abrahamic covenant, the Great Commission and the progressive growth parables of Matthew 13.
Strimple argues that the New Testament teaches one return, one resurrection and one judgment, leaving no room for an interim kingdom.
The exchange highlights disagreement over whether Old Testament prophecies of a glorious future are fulfilled before, at or after Christ's return.
Four Views on the Book of Revelation

Zondervan Counterpoints volume on how to interpret Revelation: Gentry (preterist), Hamstra (idealist), Pate (progressive dispensationalist) and Thomas (classical dispensationalist). Each essay walks through the structure and key symbols of Revelation.
Gentry argues for a pre-AD 70 date and reads the bulk of Revelation as Christ's judgment on Jerusalem.
Hamstra presents Revelation as a symbolic portrayal of timeless spiritual conflict and victory.
Pate offers an 'already/not yet' reading combining first-century fulfilment with a future consummation.
Thomas defends a consistent futurist reading of Revelation 4–22 under a literal hermeneutic.
The date of Revelation (pre-70 versus c. 95) emerges as a disputed hinge for the preterist case.
Revelation: Four Views — A Parallel Commentary
1997 (revised 2013)

A single-author reference work that sets historicist, preterist, futurist and spiritual (idealist) interpretations of each passage of Revelation in parallel columns, summarizing what representative commentators say without adjudicating. The revised edition expands the sources and adds discussion of full preterism.
Presents each school in the words and logic of its own commentators.
Introduces the date-of-Revelation debate and the major millennial views.
Shows how the same symbol (e.g. the Beast, Babylon, the 144,000) is read differently by each school.
Widely used in churches and classrooms as a neutral starting point.
Three Views on the Rapture: Pretribulation, Prewrath, or Posttribulation

Second-edition Counterpoints volume that replaces the midtribulational view with prewrath. Blaising argues for pretribulationism, Hultberg for the prewrath rapture, and Moo for posttribulationism, each with responses.
Blaising grounds pretribulationism in the Day of the Lord coming as a whole, beginning with the tribulation, from which the church is exempt (1 Thessalonians 5:9).
Hultberg argues the church endures the Antichrist's persecution but is rescued before God's wrath at the sixth seal.
Moo argues the parallels between the Olivet Discourse and Paul point to a single posttribulational coming.
All three are futurist premillennialists, so the debate is intramural.
The Rapture: Pre-, Mid-, or Post-Tribulational?

Zondervan multi-view book (later reissued as Three Views on the Rapture) in which Feinberg defends pretribulationism, Archer midtribulationism and Moo posttribulationism, with an opening history of the debate by Reiter. A contemporary Bibliotheca Sacra review called it comprehensive, scholarly and irenic.
Reiter traces the rapture debate in American evangelicalism since the Niagara Bible Conferences.
Feinberg argues the church is promised exemption from the wrath that characterizes the whole seventieth week.
Archer places the rapture at the midpoint of Daniel's seventieth week, before the great tribulation.
Moo argues for a single coming after the tribulation from Matthew 24 and 2 Thessalonians 2.
The Great Tribulation: Past or Future? Two Evangelicals Debate the Question

Kregel debate book in which Gentry argues that the great tribulation of Matthew 24 was fulfilled in the Jewish War of AD 66-70, and Ice argues that it is a future seven-year period before Christ's return. Each writes opening statements and rebuttals.
Gentry stresses 'this generation' (Matthew 24:34) and the local, Judean focus of the warnings (Matthew 24:16-20).
Ice argues 'this generation' refers to the generation that sees the signs and that the cosmic signs and global scope demand a future fulfilment.
The two disagree over whether Luke 21:20-24 interprets the 'abomination of desolation' as the Roman armies.
Both affirm a future bodily return of Christ and reject full preterism.
Covenantal and Dispensational Theologies: Four Views on the Continuity of Scripture

IVP Academic Spectrum volume comparing the four main evangelical frameworks for relating the testaments: covenant theology, progressive covenantalism, progressive dispensationalism and traditional dispensationalism. Each contributor argues and responds.
Horton presents the covenants of redemption, works and grace as the Bible's architecture.
Wellum argues that the biblical covenants progressively reach their fulfilment in Christ and the new covenant.
Bock argues for an inaugurated Davidic kingdom with a future for national Israel.
Snoeberger defends a traditional dispensational distinction between Israel and the church.
Frameworks, not just texts, shape conclusions about Israel, the land and the millennium.
Perspectives on Israel and the Church: 4 Views

B&H Academic volume on the relationship of Israel and the church: traditional covenantal (Reymond), traditional dispensational (Thomas), progressive dispensational (Saucy) and progressive covenantal (Brand and Pratt), each with responses.
Reymond sees the church as the continuation and fulfilment of true Israel.
Thomas argues for a strict distinction between Israel and the church under a grammatical-historical hermeneutic.
Saucy allows more continuity while affirming a future for national Israel.
Brand and Pratt read Israel's promises as fulfilled typologically in Christ and his people.
Three Views on Israel and the Church: Perspectives on Romans 9–11
Kregel Academic volume focused on Romans 9–11 and especially the meaning of 'all Israel will be saved' (Romans 11:26).
Vlach argues for a future mass conversion of ethnic Israel and a continuing national role for Israel.
Zaspel and Hamilton expect a future mass conversion but no separate role for Israel apart from the church.
Merkle argues Paul promises the salvation of an elect remnant throughout the age, not a future mass conversion.
The debate cuts across millennial lines: postmillennialists and many amillennialists also differ on Romans 11.
Debate on Christian Reconstruction and Dominion Theology (Dallas)

Public debate on 14 April 1988 in Dallas, hosted by Dominion Press, between dispensationalists Dave Hunt and Thomas Ice and Christian Reconstructionists Gary North and Gary DeMar. It focused on postmillennial 'dominion' and the application of biblical law. DeMar's book The Debate Over Christian Reconstruction is his summary and reply.
Ice challenged the exegetical basis of postmillennialism; Hunt criticized the Reconstructionist programme for society.
North and DeMar argued that Christ's present kingship and the Great Commission imply the progressive discipling of nations.
The debate was part of a wider late-1980s literary exchange (House and Ice, DeMar and Leithart, Bahnsen and Gentry).
Accounts come mainly from participants on each side; no neutral report of the outcome was found.
Second Dallas debate on Dominion Theology (John Ankerberg Show / NRB)

According to Thomas Ice, a second debate took place in Dallas on 29 July 1989, sponsored by The John Ankerberg Show and the National Religious Broadcasters. Greg Bahnsen was scheduled but withdrew for health reasons, so DeMar joined Gentry for the Reconstructionist side.
Continued the 1988 debate on postmillennialism and theonomy.
Gentry's participation linked the debate to his preterist-postmillennial exegesis.
Details come from Ice's own account; no transcript was located.
Preterism vs. Futurism (Biola University)

A recorded debate on 26 February 2002 at Biola University on whether the Olivet Discourse and related prophecies are past or future. It was followed by written exchanges, including DeMar's article 'On Thin Ice' and Ice's reply 'On Solid Ground'.
DeMar argued from the second-person 'you' and 'this generation' that Jesus addressed his own hearers.
Ice countered that the generic 'you' (as in Deuteronomy 4 and 30) can address the nation across generations.
DeMar's critique targeted dispensational timelines, not the hope of a future Second Coming.
Each side later disputed the other's account of what had been answered.
The Great Tribulation: Past or Future? (Ice vs. DeMar)
Thomas Ice reports a further debate with Gary DeMar on 26 May 2006 under the title 'The Great Tribulation: Past or Future?', revisiting the questions of his 1999 book with Kenneth Gentry.
Focused on whether Matthew 24:15-31 was fulfilled in AD 70.
Same title and issues as the Ice-Gentry book (1999).
Date and title come from Ice's writings; venue and recording were not confirmed.
An Evening of Eschatology

A two-hour moderated roundtable held 27 September 2009 at Bethlehem Baptist Church in Minneapolis, sponsored by Desiring God and Bethlehem College & Seminary. Hamilton (historic premillennial), Storms (amillennial) and Wilson (postmillennial) presented and cross-examined one another; Piper said he holds historic premillennialism and regards amillennialism as the next most plausible view.
Hamilton read Revelation 19–20 sequentially, with the millennium following Christ's return.
Storms read Revelation 20 as the present reign of Christ and departed saints, recapitulating the church age.
Wilson argued that Christ reigns now and the gospel will progressively disciple the nations before his return.
A notably irenic example of all three millennial views debated by Reformed evangelicals together.
Dr. Brown Debates Gary DeMar on Israel and the Church
undated (online by 2021)

Audio debate hosted by The Line of Fire on 'replacement theology', Israel's role in prophecy and God's future purposes for the Jewish people. Brown, a Messianic Jewish historic premillennialist, defended a distinct future for ethnic Israel; DeMar, a postmillennial partial preterist, argued that the church is the continuation of true Israel while rejecting the 'replacement' label.
Disagreement centred on Romans 11 and the Old Testament restoration promises.
Brown stressed promised national deliverance and the embrace of the Messiah by Israel.
DeMar stressed New Testament fulfilment of Israel's hopes in Christ.
Date and full content were not confirmed.
Dr. Brown Debates Don Preston on Romans 11
undated

Line of Fire debate in which full preterist Don Preston argued that the salvation of 'all Israel' in Romans 11 was fulfilled by AD 70, and Brown argued for a still-future national turning of Israel to the Messiah tied to Christ's future return.
Centred on Romans 11:25-27 and its citation of Isaiah 59.
Preston links the 'coming of the Deliverer' to the AD 70 consummation of the old covenant.
Brown affirms a future bodily return and resurrection, which Preston denies.
Dr. Brown Debates Michael Sullivan on Full Preterism

Line of Fire debate in which Sullivan, a 'sovereign grace' full preterist, argued that the Second Coming, resurrection and judgment were fulfilled at the end of the old covenant age in AD 70; Brown defended the historic expectation of a future bodily return and resurrection.
Sullivan builds on New Testament time-statements ('at hand', 'this generation').
Brown appeals to bodily-resurrection texts such as 1 Corinthians 15 and the creedal consensus.
Illustrates how full preterism is engaged by premillennialists as well as by Reformed postmillennialists and amillennialists.
Dominion Theology: Blessing or Curse? and House Divided (print exchange)

A book-length printed debate. House and Ice (Multnomah, 1988) critiqued theonomy and Reconstructionist postmillennialism from a dispensational perspective; Bahnsen and Gentry replied point by point in House Divided: The Break-Up of Dispensational Theology (1989), defending theonomic postmillennialism and criticizing dispensationalism.
House and Ice argued that the Mosaic law does not bind the nations today and that the church age ends in apostasy, not triumph.
Bahnsen defended the continuing validity of God's law; Gentry defended postmillennial exegesis.
Ice had himself been a theonomist until 1986, which lent the exchange intensity.
Each side regarded the other's book as a decisive answer.
The Apocalypse Code and Breaking the Apocalypse Code (print exchange)

Hanegraaff's The Apocalypse Code (2007) attacked the Left Behind style of dispensational futurism and proposed an 'exegetical eschatology' reading much of Revelation as fulfilled in AD 70. Ice reviewed it critically and, with Mark Hitchcock, published Breaking the Apocalypse Code in reply.
Hanegraaff argued for an early date of Revelation and against Christian Zionism.
Ice and Hitchcock argued that Hanegraaff misrepresented Tim LaHaye and abandoned a literal hermeneutic.
Both sides affirm a future bodily return and resurrection.
Publisher and year of the Ice-Hitchcock book were not confirmed online.
When Shall These Things Be? A Reformed Response to Hyper-Preterism

A multi-author Reformed critique of full ('hyper') preterism by amillennial and postmillennial scholars, addressing creeds, history, hermeneutics, the resurrection and the Second Coming. Full preterists published replies arguing that the critics did not answer the time-texts.
Argues that the creeds' affirmation of future return and resurrection reflects the church's universal reading of Scripture.
Several chapters examine the resurrection texts (1 Corinthians 15) and argue they require a future bodily resurrection.
Gentry argues that partial preterists can consistently distinguish AD 70 from the final coming.
Notable as postmillennialists and amillennialists jointly opposing full preterism.
He Shall Have Dominion: A Postmillennial Eschatology

Widely regarded as the most comprehensive modern defense of postmillennialism, combining biblical theology of the covenants, exegesis of Old Testament kingdom prophecies and the Great Commission, and a preterist reading of the Olivet Discourse and Revelation.
Traces a theme of redemptive victory from Genesis 3:15 through the Abrahamic and Davidic covenants.
Reads Psalm 110 and 1 Corinthians 15:24-26 as Christ reigning until his enemies are subdued before his return.
Argues the kingdom grows gradually like leaven and mustard seed (Matthew 13).
Answers objections drawn from texts on apostasy and suffering.
Before Jerusalem Fell: Dating the Book of Revelation

A detailed argument for a Neronic date of Revelation (c. AD 65–66), examining external evidence (including the interpretation of Irenaeus) and internal evidence (the temple in Revelation 11, the seven kings of Revelation 17). The date is disputed; late-date scholars such as Beale and Hitchcock reply that the external evidence for c. AD 95 is strong.
Argues Irenaeus's statement may refer to John, not the vision, being seen under Domitian (a disputed reading).
Reads Revelation 11:1-2 as presupposing the temple still standing.
Identifies the sixth king of Revelation 17:10 with Nero.
Links 666 to the gematria of 'Nero Caesar' in Hebrew letters.
A Case for Amillennialism: Understanding the End Times
2003 (expanded 2013)
An accessible defense of amillennialism as the historic Protestant view, organized around the 'two-age' structure of New Testament eschatology and Christ's present reign.
Argues that 'this age' and 'the age to come' leave no room for an interim millennium.
Reads Revelation 20 as recapitulating the church age.
Critiques dispensational and postmillennial readings of Daniel 9 and Romans 11.
Explains the 'already/not yet' as tension between present victory and present suffering.
Kingdom Come: The Amillennial Alternative

A thorough exegetical defense of amillennialism by a former dispensationalist, covering Daniel's seventy weeks, the Olivet Discourse, Romans 11, 2 Thessalonians 2 and Revelation 20, with chapters interacting with premillennialism and postmillennialism.
Argues that 1 Corinthians 15:23-26 places the defeat of death at Christ's return, ruling out post-return death in a millennium.
Reads Revelation 20:1-3 as Satan restrained from deceiving the nations during the gospel age.
Accepts preterist readings of much of the Olivet Discourse.
Critiques postmillennialism for underweighting suffering in the present age.
The Bible and the Future
A standard Reformed textbook on eschatology covering both personal and cosmic eschatology, notable for 'inaugurated eschatology' and its emphasis on the new earth.
Argues that the New Testament presents the end as already begun in Christ.
Argues the final hope is a renewed earth, not an ethereal heaven.
Prefers 'realized millennialism' as a positive label for amillennialism.
Includes critiques of dispensational premillennialism.
A Case for Historic Premillennialism: An Alternative to 'Left Behind' Eschatology
A multi-author case for premillennialism without dispensational distinctives and with a posttribulational rapture, drawing on church history, the Old Testament, the Gospels, Paul and Revelation.
Argues the early church's chiliasm was historic premillennial, not dispensational.
Reads Revelation 19–20 sequentially, with two bodily resurrections.
Rejects a pretribulational rapture in favour of a single return.
Presents the view as a middle way between dispensationalism and amillennialism.
Things to Come: A Study in Biblical Eschatology
The classic comprehensive textbook of classical dispensational eschatology, covering hermeneutics, the biblical covenants, the rapture, Daniel's seventieth week, the millennium and the eternal state.
Argues for a consistent literal hermeneutic as the basis of premillennialism.
Treats the Abrahamic, Davidic and New covenants as unconditional promises to national Israel.
Defends a pretribulational rapture.
Describes the millennium as the fulfilment of Israel's kingdom promises.
Progressive Dispensationalism

The defining statement of progressive dispensationalism, which sees the dispensations as progressive stages in one plan and the Davidic kingdom as already inaugurated, while retaining a future for Israel and a premillennial return.
Argues Christ now reigns on David's throne at the Father's right hand (Acts 2:30-36).
Sees the church as a stage in, not a parenthesis to, the kingdom programme.
Maintains a future national and territorial restoration of Israel.
Moves toward a holistic new-creation eschatology.
Kingdom through Covenant: A Biblical-Theological Understanding of the Covenants
A major biblical-theological study of the covenants proposing 'progressive covenantalism' as a middle way between covenant theology and dispensationalism.
Traces the covenants from creation to the new covenant as the backbone of the biblical story.
Argues typology escalates to fulfilment in Christ.
Reads Israel's land promise as fulfilled in the new creation.
Rejects both a single covenant of grace and a separate future plan for national Israel.

A systematic study of every New Testament reference to Christ's coming, concluding that all were fulfilled within the apostolic generation, culminating in AD 70. It is the founding classic of full preterism and is also cited by partial preterists for its time-text analysis. Critics note that its conclusions deny the creedal future bodily resurrection and return.
Treats the time-statements ('soon', 'at hand', 'this generation') as decisive.
Reads the Olivet Discourse, Thessalonians and Revelation as one prophetic horizon.
Applies the resurrection and judgment to the AD 70 transition.
Remains in print and influential among full and partial preterists.
The Puritan Hope: Revival and the Interpretation of Prophecy

A historical study of the eschatological hope of the English and Scottish Puritans and their heirs, centred on the future conversion of the Jews (Romans 11) and the worldwide spread of the gospel, and its role in the modern missionary movement.
